name: Stranger Trees
description: Will shares a psychic connection with the Upside Down Monster, so everything the monster knows, Will knows. Suddenly, he started drawing, page after page, non-stop. Joyce, his mom, and Chief Hopper put the drawings together, and they realized, it's a labeled tree! A tree is a connected acyclic graph. Will's tree has n vertices. Joyce and Hopper don't know what that means, so they're investigating this tree and similar trees. For each k such that 0 ≤ k ≤ n - 1 , they're going to investigate all labeled trees with n vertices that share exactly k edges with Will's tree. Two labeled trees are different if and only if there's a pair of vertices ( v , u ) such that there's an edge between v and u in one tree and not in the other one. Hopper and Joyce want to know how much work they have to do, so they asked you to tell them the number of labeled trees with n vertices that share exactly k edges with Will's tree, for each k . The answer could be very large, so they only asked you to tell them the answers modulo 1000000007 = 10 9 + 7 .
input_specification: The first line of input contains a single integer n ( 2 ≤ n ≤ 100 ) — the size of the tree. The next n - 1 lines contain the edges of Will's tree. Each line contains two integers v and u ( 1 ≤ v , u ≤ n , v ≠ u ), endpoints of an edge. It is guaranteed that the given graph is a tree.
output_specification: Print n integers in one line. i -th integer should be the number of the number of labeled trees with n vertices that share exactly i - 1 edges with Will's tree, modulo 1000 000 007 = 10 9 + 7 .
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 917D — Stranger Trees [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
